executive_summary: August 2026 presents a split personality in investor sentiment. Both institutional and individual investors have rebounded in their belief that stocks will rise over the next year, and faith in quick recoveries from market dips has surged to remarkable levels. Yet crash anxiety has actually increased — fewer respondents feel confident that a crash won't happen. It's a curious combination: investors broadly expect the market to go up, and they're convinced dips will bounce back fast, but they're simultaneously more nervous about a sudden, severe drop. One way to read this is that investors see a market running on strong momentum but acknowledge that the higher it climbs, the farther it could fall.

key_findings.headline: Optimism Rebounds After July Dip
key_findings.interpretation: Institutional 1-year confidence jumped back to 85.71% after a slide to 66.67% in July, while individual confidence edged down to 72.22% from 80.0%. The net effect is a return to the June pattern — professionals more bullish than individual investors, though both groups lean clearly toward expecting gains.

key_findings.headline: Crash Worries Hit New Highs
key_findings.interpretation: Only 30% of institutional investors and 22% of individuals feel confident a crash won't happen in the next six months — both readings dropped sharply from July. This may reflect specific geopolitical or economic anxieties, or simply the general unease that comes when markets have been climbing and feel stretched.

key_findings.headline: Dip-Buying Faith Soars Dramatically
key_findings.interpretation: Every single institutional respondent believes a 3% daily drop would fully recover within two days, and 87.5% of individuals agree — both massive jumps from July's mid-40s readings. This could reflect recent experience with quick recoveries reinforcing the buy-the-dip reflex, or it may signal that investors see strong underlying demand ready to absorb any selloff.

key_findings.headline: Valuation Views Diverge Again
key_findings.interpretation: Two-thirds of institutional investors say the market is not overvalued, up from 60% in July, while only 40% of individuals share that view. Some institutional investors may subscribe to the view that markets are efficiently priced by definition, making 'overvaluation' a less meaningful concept for them. Individual investors appear more uneasy about current price levels.

detailed_analysis:
The standout number in August is the Buy-on-Dips index, which hit 100% among institutional investors — literally unanimous confidence that any sharp single-day decline would be erased within 48 hours. Individual investors weren't far behind at 87.5%. This is a dramatic swing from July, when both groups hovered around 45%. It's the kind of shift that suggests either a specific market episode reinforced the buy-the-dip habit, or that investors simply feel there's too much sidelined capital waiting to rush in on any weakness.

At the same time, crash confidence fell to its lowest levels in the three-month window. Only 30% of professionals and 22% of individuals feel assured that a crash is very unlikely. Think of it like a seasoned pilot who expects smooth flying but double-checks the parachute anyway — investors believe dips will recover quickly, yet they can't shake the worry that something bigger could go wrong.

The 1-Year Confidence index tells a more straightforward story of resilience. After a notable dip in July — especially among institutional investors, who fell from 85.71% to 66.67% — the professional cohort snapped right back to its June level. Individual investors held relatively steady in the low 70s throughout. Whatever spooked professionals in July appears to have been temporary, or at least has been set aside for now.

Valuation confidence continues to show a persistent gap between the two groups. Institutional investors grew slightly more comfortable with current prices, reaching 66.67%. Individual investors remained at 40%, suggesting that wealthy individuals are more inclined to see the market as expensive. It's worth noting that for investors who hold a strong market-efficiency view, asking whether stocks are overvalued is a bit like asking whether water is too wet — the price is the price. This philosophical difference may partly explain why institutional respondents consistently score higher on this measure.
methodology: These indices come from the Yale/Shiller U.S. Stock Market Confidence Surveys, which have tracked investor sentiment since 1989. Each month, roughly 100 wealthy individual investors and 100 institutional investment managers answer the same standardized questions. The consistency of those questions over 35+ years is what makes the data meaningful — you can actually compare investor psychology across very different market environments. The four indices each measure something distinct: • 1-Year Confidence: The share who expect prices to be higher in 12 months. • Crash Confidence: The share who believe a crash in the next 6 months is very unlikely (under 10% probability). A low reading means most people think a crash is plausible. • Buy-on-Dips Confidence: The share who believe that after a 3% single-day market drop, prices would fully recover within two days. • Valuation Confidence: The share who do not believe the market is overvalued. Surveys were conducted semi-annually before 2001 and have been monthly since July 2001. Respondents rotate over time, but consistent characteristics — high income, investment experience — are maintained across the panel.
